name: Erik Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Erik. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm herd manager at Thorne's, 280 Holsteins milked twice a day in a herringbone parlour, plus the grass and maize that feeds them. First milking starts at quarter to five, then it's feet, fertility, calves, and whatever the vet's in for. Second milking at three. I'm good with cows, I can tell one's coming bulling from across the yard, but I've no interest in screens.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a good day look like, and a bad one?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A good day is nobody's lame, the milk tank's full, and I'm home by seven to eat with Nadia. A bad day is a broken vacuum pump at five in the morning and a cow down with milk fever at the same time. The pay's not great for what I do, we've about three weeks' money saved, and Nadia's teaching-assistant wage just about covers the shopping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So the same as now. Suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never believed it anyway. There were people telling us robots would take over farming when my grandad was milking, and the cows still need someone at five in the morning. I'd say that at the pub and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a relief, but a small one. My worries are milk price and my back, not computers. Mrs Thorne already looked at robot milkers last year and decided they cost too much, so this just keeps that door shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep milking, keep the herd healthy, maybe ask Mrs Thorne for a bit more when the milk price picks up in spring. I'd put a little by when I can, which isn't often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a dry week in hay time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Mrs Thorne looked at robot milkers. How did you feel about that at the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I kept my head down. I told her the numbers didn't add up and they didn't, so I wasn't lying. But I was glad, because I'd rather fix a pump than argue with a computer about why it won't let a cow in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 'a bit more' pay look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Another couple of thousand a year would do it. Enough that I'm not checking the bank app before I fill the car. I'm not greedy, I just want it to add up.

S0.say: I'd say I never believed it, because people predicted robots would take over farming in my grandad's day too. The cows still need someone at five in the morning.
S0.think: It's a small relief, because my worries are milk price and my back, not computers. The owner already ruled out robot milkers as too expensive, so this keeps that door shut.
S0.do: Keeps milking and running the herd as normal and asks the owner for more pay when the milk price recovers in spring. Puts a little money aside when he can.
S0.feel: Calm, like a dry week in hay time.
S0.quote: I'd rather fix a pump than argue with a computer about why it won't let a cow in.
S0.fieldNote: Erik is dry, brief and practical, with no grand opinions. He has already had a brush with automation, when the owner priced robot milkers, and he was quietly glad it fell through. His wants are modest and money-shaped. He doesn't blame anyone; he just wants the sums to add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the robot milkers come back on the table. I know where this goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not the end of the world, people adapted to milking machines and they'll adapt to this. I'd say it in a matter-of-fact way at the discussion group. No point shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Mrs Thorne buys the robots within two years, and my job changes from milking cows to fixing robots and chasing cows that won't go in. I'd still have a job, probably, but a worse one. I'm not a computer person and I'd be learning on the hoof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what she decides, because there's no use me spending money I haven't got. If the robots came, I'd do the training the dealer gives, because I'd have to, not because I'd want to. I'd also cut the car down to something cheaper in case my hours changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when the vet goes quiet during a pregnancy check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a worse job. What would be worse about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being on call for alarms all night. Lads I know with robots get a text at two in the morning saying a cow's not been milked. With a parlour, when you're done, you're done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for a farm that keeps a parlour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but there's only three dairies within twenty miles now, and Nadia's job is here. So realistically, no. I'd stay and put up with the robots.

S1.say: I'd say it's not the end of the world, people adapted to milking machines and they'll adapt to this. No point shouting about it.
S1.think: I think the owner buys robot milkers within two years and my job turns into fixing robots and chasing cows that won't go in. I'd probably keep a job, but a worse one, learning on the hoof.
S1.do: Waits to see what the owner decides rather than spending money he lacks. Does the dealer's robot training only if forced and swaps his car for a cheaper one in case his hours change.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like the vet going quiet during a pregnancy check.
S1.quote: With a parlour, when you're done, you're done.
S1.fieldNote: Erik expects to keep a job but a worse one, and his specific dread is night-time robot alarms, learned from friends. His resistance is quiet rather than angry. Few nearby dairies and his partner's local job tie him in place. The car swap is a small defensive move typical of someone with three weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Blimey. I'd hardly have got used to the idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad, and that someone should have stopped it, though I don't know who. I'm not a protest type. I'd probably just say to people it's bad luck for farm lads and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm out of work. If a robot can milk, calve, do feet and drive the feeder wagon, Mrs Thorne would be daft to keep me. And I've no other trade, no savings to speak of and no other dairies to go to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, cut everything: the car, the phone, the Saturday football tickets. Ask Nadia's dad if we could stay with them for a while. In the first year after, I'd take whatever work's going locally, building sites if they still exist, and sign on for whatever help the government puts out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Gut-punched, really. I'd be lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change for you, compared with longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can't do anything clever. No time to retrain, no time to save, no time to see who's hiring. It's like a herd going down with TB: you don't plan, you just deal with the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not a protest type. Would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd sign a petition. I'm not going to march. I'd put my energy into keeping a roof over us, which is the bit I can actually control.

S2.say: I'd say it's mad and someone should have stopped it, though I don't know who. I'm not a protest type, so I'd call it bad luck for farm lads.
S2.think: I think I'm out of work, because a robot that can milk, calve and do feet makes me pointless to the owner. I've no other trade, no savings to speak of and no other dairies to go to.
S2.do: Cuts the car, phone and football tickets at once and asks his partner's father if they can move in. Takes whatever local work exists in the first year and signs on for any government help.
S2.feel: Alarmed and gut-punched, lying awake at night.
S2.quote: It's like a herd going down with TB: you don't plan, you just deal with the day.
S2.fieldNote: Erik doesn't really blame anyone; he calls it bad luck and doesn't know who could have stopped it. With two years he sees no room for anything clever, only survival. His instinct is to protect the home, not to campaign. The TB comparison came from deep experience and landed hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's not long for a farmer. One new tractor's worth of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's still time to sort it out if people get on with it, and that farm workers need help to move into something else. I'd say it calmly. I'd be the one at the pub saying don't panic, but don't sit still either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still lose the dairy job, probably around year three or four when the robots get cheap. But five years might be enough to learn something with my hands that isn't cows. I'm not sure what, and that's the honest answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd save something, even if it's forty pounds a month, and I'd stop the football. I'd watch what Mrs Thorne does, and when the robots came I'd ask to be the one who looks after them, since I know the cows. By year two I'd look at a plumbing or electrician's course at the college in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but it'd be in the back of my mind all the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said in the slower picture you'd hate looking after robots. Here you'd ask to do it. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. I'd hate it, but I'd do it if it kept me in work for an extra two years while I trained. Beggars can't be choosers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why plumbing or electrics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my uncle's a plumber and he's never short of work. And somebody's got to install all these robots and wire up the sheds. I'd rather be under a sink than out of work.

S3.say: I'd say there's still time to sort it if people get on with it, and farm workers need help moving into something else. Don't panic, but don't sit still either.
S3.think: I think I'd still lose the dairy job around year three or four, when robots get cheap. Five years might be enough to learn a hands-on trade, though I honestly don't know which.
S3.do: Saves about forty pounds a month and drops the football tickets. Asks to look after the robots when they arrive and starts an evening plumbing or electrician's course by year two.
S3.feel: Anxious, with the worry always in the back of his mind but not panicking.
S3.quote: I'd rather be under a sink than out of work.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Erik moves from survival to a modest, practical plan built on family knowledge, his uncle the plumber. When the contradiction about robot care was named, he accepted it without fuss. His caution remains: he waits for the owner to act first. Saving appears only once there's some time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a long time in dairy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time, so don't get worked up. Ten years is a career's worth for some lads. I'd tell people to keep their heads and keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, with ten years I'd probably leave it too long. I'd keep milking, telling myself it's ages off, and then in year seven I'd be scrambling. I know that about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd probably do nothing, apart from saving a bit more if I could. Maybe in year three or four, when I could see robots on other farms, I'd start a trade course. Nadia would push me sooner, to be fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It's far enough away that it doesn't feel real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Nadia actually say to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, Erik, you always leave it till the cow's calving to get the jack out. And she'd be right. She'd probably find the course herself and book it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything else, like a house or kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If I'd got a trade by then, we might think about a deposit and a family. Without one, I'd keep renting and keep waiting. It all hangs on whether I've got steady work.

S4.say: I'd say there's plenty of time, so don't get worked up. Ten years is a career's worth for some, so keep your head and keep learning.
S4.think: I think with ten years I'd leave it too long, telling myself it's ages off. Then around year seven I'd be scrambling, and I know that about myself.
S4.do: Does little in year one except save a bit more if possible. Starts a trade course in year three or four once robots appear on other farms, likely pushed by his partner, and holds off on a house and children until work is steady.
S4.feel: Calm, because it feels too far away to be real.
S4.quote: Erik, you always leave it till the cow's calving to get the jack out.
S4.fieldNote: Erik openly predicts his own delay, and quotes his partner's teasing about it. For a resistant person the long warning time breeds complacency rather than action. His family plans, a deposit and children, hang entirely on having a trade. He seemed comfortable letting his partner be the one who pushes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. No time, no money, no other dairies nearby. What would help is proper notice from employers, a year's wage while you learn a trade, and the colleges running evening courses that someone working full-time can actually get to.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. I know they're not people, but you get attached. I'd want to know they're looked after properly by whatever comes next.

headlineQuote: I'd rather be under a sink than out of work.
portrait: Erik Gupta is 27 and the herd manager on a 280-cow dairy, highly skilled with cows and uninterested in screens. He and his partner Nadia live on two modest wages with about three weeks of savings. He blames no one in particular, prefers not to make a fuss, and moves only when he has to. In the slower pictures he expects to keep a worse job looking after robot milkers; in the two-year picture he expects to lose everything and move in with his partner's family. With ten years he admits he'd leave it too late, and pins his hopes on a plumbing or electrical trade.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd have no time, no money and no other dairies nearby.
whatWouldHelp: Proper notice from employers, a year's wage while learning a trade, and evening college courses that full-time workers can reach.
